meta.title: Who really said "Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Nobody, quite. Eric Roth wrote "life WAS like a box of chocolates" for Forrest Gump (1994). The famous version splices two different lines from the film.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is misquoted. Forrest says "was like"; his mother says "is a box of chocolates". The popular wording blends the two — and isn't in the novel.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “life was like a box of chocolates”
answer.authorDates: b. 22 March 1945 · American screenwriter · Academy Award, Best Adapted Screenplay (1994)
answer.sourceLine: Screenwriter Eric Roth wrote the line for the 1994 film Forrest Gump, where Forrest (Tom Hanks) says “My Momma always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get.” The popular version swaps the past tense for the present and drops the attribution to Momma — and, per Wikiquote’s transcription ↗, no one in the film says “life is like a box of chocolates” at all.

source.excerpt: My Momma always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get.
trail: The transcription. Wikiquote’s page for the film ↗ gives Forrest’s line as “My Momma always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get,” notes its AFI ranking, and separately records Mrs. Gump’s “Life is a box of chocolates, Forrest.” It also credits the film as “Written by Eric Roth, based on the novel by Winston Groom.”

Independent confirmation of the tense. AFI’s 100 Years…100 Movie Quotes ↗ ranks the line #40 and prints it “My mama always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get” — attributed to Forrest Gump, Tom Hanks, 1994. Two independent transcriptions, same past tense.

Origination. Wikipedia’s article on the film ↗ credits the screenplay to Eric Roth, adapting Groom’s novel, and quotes Zemeckis on how far Roth departed from the book. This Day in Quotes ↗ gives the novel’s own chocolate line — “bein a idiot is no box of chocolates” — which carries a nearly opposite sense. The film originated the quotation; the novel supplied only the image.

A note on what we could not check. Quote Investigator has no article on this quote (searched July 2026), so there is no specialist anchor to defer to here. Snopes has a fact-check at snopes.com/fact-check/forrest-gump-mandela-effect whose title alone frames the same “was like” finding, but the page would not serve to us and we have not cited it as support for any claim on this page.
source.excerptNote: That is Forrest’s line as transcribed at Wikiquote ↗. Earlier in the film his mother gives it in a different form — “Life is a box of chocolates, Forrest. You never know what you’re gonna get” — present tense, but without “like.” Those are the only two chocolate lines Wikiquote records, and the popular “Life is like a box of chocolates” matches neither. Transcriptions differ on small points of Forrest’s accent (Wikiquote has “My Momma”; AFI prints “My mama”; some renderings give “box a chocolates”), but every source consulted agrees on the word that matters: was.
source.rightsNote: Forrest Gump was released in 1994 and is firmly in copyright in the United States — US public domain currently reaches only works published through 1930. Screenwriting is work-for-hire, so the copyright in the screenplay sits with the studio rather than with Eric Roth personally; Paramount Pictures ↗ distributed the film. Winston Groom’s underlying 1986 novel (Doubleday) is separately in copyright.

author.name: Eric Roth

author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Eric Roth (born 22 March 1945 in New York City) is an American screenwriter who won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for Forrest Gump (1994). His later credits include The Insider, Munich, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, A Star Is Born, Dune and Killers of the Flower Moon. Roth departed substantially from Winston Groom’s source novel — director Robert Zemeckis noted that the book was “cynical and colder than the movie” — and the chocolates line as audiences know it is Roth’s writing, not Groom’s.

misattribution.heading: What actually went wrong here
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited with this line — the film is right and Eric Roth is right. What drifted is the wording, plus two related errors about where the line came from and who authored it.

items.why: The film has the past tense. Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ gives Forrest’s line as “My Momma always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get,” and AFI’s list ↗, which ranks it #40, also renders it “was like.” The popular version additionally drops “My Momma always said,” which is what makes it past tense in the first place.

Earlier in the film Forrest’s mother says, per Wikiquote ↗, “Life is a box of chocolates, Forrest. You never know what you’re gonna get.” Present tense — but a metaphor, with no “like.” Between them the two characters supply every word of the popular quotation; neither one says it.

The line is often assumed to come from the book the film adapted. It does not. This Day in Quotes ↗ gives the novel’s chocolate line as “Let me say this: bein a idiot is no box of chocolates” — a grievance about mistreatment, not a meditation on uncertainty. The famous line is Roth’s invention for the screenplay.

Hanks is the actor and Forrest is a fictional character; neither wrote the words. The author of a screen line is the screenwriter — here Eric Roth ↗, who won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for it.

misattribution.truthLine: The real line is “My Momma always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get” — written by Eric Roth for Forrest Gump (1994), spoken by Tom Hanks, and ranked #40 by the American Film Institute ↗. It is not from Winston Groom’s novel.

context.heading: A misquote spliced from two real lines
lead: Most misquotes are a single sentence worn smooth by repetition. This one is unusual: it looks like a merger. In the film, Forrest’s mother says it first — “Life is a box of chocolates, Forrest. You never know what you’re gonna get” — present tense, but a metaphor, not a simile. Later, on the bench, Forrest reports it back in the past tense and adds the missing word: “My Momma always said life was like a box of chocolates.” The version the world repeats takes the present tense from her and the “like” from him, and belongs to neither.

The tense is not a trivial casualty. “Life was like a box of chocolates” is reported speech — Forrest quoting a dead woman, on a bench, to a stranger. The line is doing grief and memory work, not dispensing a maxim. Flattened to “life is like,” it becomes exactly the free-floating fortune-cookie aphorism the scene was built to avoid, which is presumably why it travelled so well onto mugs and posters.
context.detailsSummary: Where the metaphor actually came from
detailsBody: The chocolate image does trace back to Winston Groom’s 1986 novel, but the sentiment there is close to the opposite. This Day in Quotes ↗ gives Groom’s line as “Let me say this: bein a idiot is no box of chocolates” — a complaint about how the world treats him, not a reflection on life’s unpredictability. (Transcriptions of Groom’s dialect spelling vary between editions and quote sites; the sense is consistent even where the spelling is not.)

So the direction of borrowing here is the reverse of the usual case. Roth did not lift a finished line from the novel and sharpen it, the way the Gone with the Wind screenplay added one word to Mitchell’s “My dear, I don’t give a damn.” He took a bitter throwaway image and rebuilt it into something warm and load-bearing. The film is genuinely the origin of the quotation — the novel supplied only the chocolates.
context.pull: The famous version takes the tense from the mother and the simile from the son — and belongs to neither.
